title: Same light in all
hook: temple and mosque are the same, the forms of worship the same, all people one, though they look different (Akal Ustat 86)

segments.voice: Yesterday, one human race: manas ki jat sabhai ekai pahichanbo, recognize the whole human race as one. Which stranger did you greet like a cousin? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-five.

In an anatomy class, the body on the table has no religion. The instructor points: here are the eyes, here the ears, here the lungs that took in air, here the heart. Nobody in the room can tell, from any of it, how this person prayed or which festival they loved. The next stanza of Akal Ustat goes to that same table. It names the places people pray, the clothes they wear, and then it looks underneath.
screen: `THE BODY ON THE TABLE.` → `EYES, EARS, LUNGS, HEART.` → `THE STANZA LOOKS UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: Akal Ustat, the very next stanza, in paraphrase. The temple and the mosque are the same; the Hindu worship and the Muslim prayer are the same. All people are one, though they appear many. Then a list of beings and peoples, and the reason they look different: it's the dress and custom of different lands. Then the anatomy lesson. The same eyes, the same ears, the same body, the same build. Each one a mix of earth and air, fire and water. And the stanza closes by setting names for God and books side by side and calling them the same. Yesterday's stanza was about the word for the human family. Today's is about what you see. Difference is real, the stanza says; it's the way a land dresses its people. But the eye and the ear and the four elements are shared. So the title for today, same light, is the stanza's conclusion carried one step: if the body is one stuff, the light that lives in it is one too. That's one way Sikhs read it, and it echoes a line in Sohila, in the Guru Granth Sahib: the One's light is in all. And this is a week's end, so look how the week has climbed. The world as a dream we wake from gently. The Name that remains when the dream ends. The Gurus' teachings closing, one teaching in many voices. Then a new block: the book of the Tenth, discussed with respect. Akal Ustat, praise that puts armies in scale. One human race. And now, under every robe and every rooftop, the same light.
screen: `TEMPLE AND MOSQUE, THE SAME.` · `DIFFERENT DRESS OF DIFFERENT LANDS.` · `SAME EYES, EARS, EARTH AND WATER.` · `A WEEK FROM DREAM TO LIGHT.` · then, large: `ALL THE SAME LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see sameness beneath difference. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who looks, dresses or prays very differently from you. Let the differences be there; don't paint over them. Then look underneath, the way the stanza does. Their eyes. Their ears. Breath coming in and going out, the same air you're breathing right now. Hold both at once: the dress of a land, and the same light. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
Same light in all. Temple and mosque, worship and prayer, different dress of different lands, and underneath, the same eyes, the same body, the same light. Today's word.
Your line: all the same light. Today, when someone's clothes or customs catch your eye, look one layer down. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing and recite this stanza of Akal Ustat in kirtan and quote it when speaking of the oneness of humankind; it is read as teaching that one divine light lives in every person.

match.prompt: the stanza says: tap the pairs.

myth: the stanza says people look different because they are different kinds of being
it says the difference is the dress and custom of different lands.
the stanza reaches for the body to make its point
same eyes, same ears, same body, a mix of earth, air, fire and water.
the stanza asks people to stop worshiping in their own way
it calls temple and mosque the same; it doesn't ask anyone to leave either.

fork.setup: you're looking at two people who dress and pray very differently. what does the stanza tell you to see?
options: the dress of a land, and underneath, the same body and the same light.
fork.reveal: it names the difference honestly, then points underneath: the same eyes, ears and elements.

original.note: light, the divine light Sikhs speak of as present in every being.

trapdoor: what you thought: saying temple and mosque are the same means difference doesn't matter.
what it means: the stanza names the difference as the dress of lands, and finds one body and one light underneath.
what a scholar hears: it argues from the body itself: the same eyes, ears, build, and earth, air, fire and water.
